html:
The classic chicken or egg dilemma. Which comes first? Acquiring more clients or hiring more financial advisors? There is a natural tendency to hold off on hiring new talent until you see the goods. However, firms with a service centered model can actually grow their business by adding more financial advisors to their team. Here’s why.

New Hire, New Network

Word of mouth and referrals are still king in attracting new business. According to Nielsen, 92% of consumers believe suggestions from friends and family more than advertising. No matter the experience level, a good financial advisor will bring a whole new network of people to the business. Clients will often follow a senior advisor to a new firm. Junior advisors are hungry to build their network. Plus, they may have access to younger clients that can be cultivated now to ensure a healthy client pipeline in the future.

More Personal Attention

If your digital marketing and referral strategies are bringing in new business, that’s great. But, if you’re overloading your existing advisors with these new clients, customer service is going to suffer. Clients have high expectations about customer service these days regardless of the level of assets. Missing a call can mean losing a client. Adding new talent allows the whole team to work with a manageable client list and provide a high level of personal attention. The return is growth and retention.

Fresh Perspective

With any new hire comes fresh ideas and new perspectives. Senior advisors may offer effective best practices learned at a previous firm. Junior advisors may be more tech-savvy and offer new growth strategies in the digital landscape. A fresh pair of eyes on any established business can help identify blindspots and advance solutions.

As firms develop growth strategies in 2022, it would be wise to examine the benefits of hiring new talent. Marketing plans can include hiring benchmarks as various strategies are rolled out. Ultimately, the chicken and the egg go together. Marketing efforts and hiring advisors should be envisioned in harmony with each other.

html:
Most adults in the United States skipped “Money Management 101” and it’s causing a crisis. According to the NFEC, financial illiteracy cost Americans roughly $352 Billion collectively in 2021. With financial literacy in a downward spiral, financial advisors are being called upon to pick up the slack. In order to serve clients and the larger community, money managers are having to play a lot of different roles.

The Therapist

Money is an emotional issue for almost everyone under normal circumstances. Combine that with economic uncertainty and financial illiteracy, and you have the perfect recipe for shame, denial, and anxiety. As a culture, Americans are taught not to talk about money. A CNBC article revealed “44% of Americans surveyed would rather discuss death, religion or politics than talk about personal finance with a loved one.” Before any investing or planning can take place, financial advisors have to first establish trust, break through the wall of silence, and diffuse any fears or anxiety.

The Teacher

When 60% of adults don’t use a budget, financial advisors have their work cut out for them explaining complex investment concepts. They have to first assess their client’s financial knowledge. Then, start filling in the gaps by giving them smart financial tools (like a budget) and breaking down industry jargon into easily digestible information. Teaching clients also helps with the emotional side of financial planning. Clients often feel more engaged and confident when they are learning something they didn’t know before.

The Community Leader

In most states, personal finance courses are not required for high school students. Even if they have access to these courses the majority of students are not taking them. Given their expertise, financial advisors are being encouraged to fill in the gap by volunteering in their local communities, offering free online seminars, or advocating for government programs.

Long gone are the days when just being a good financial analyst qualified you as a good financial advisor. Now, money managers need to add the roles of therapist, teacher, and community leader to their professional profile.
